source.title: Finding "misaligned persona" features in open-weight models

record.file_problem: The post text is present. Plot captions are included, but numerical values shown only in the plots are not available.
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes open-weight instruct models on a narrow harmful task and evaluates unrelated prompts using the evaluation from Betley et al.; it also tests feature ablation on that behavior.
record.gate_note: The post reports that bad-medical-advice fine-tunes induce misalignment and good-medical-advice fine-tunes do not, but the plotted rates are not available as numbers. It also reports ablation outcomes in text without numerical rates. Feature cosine scores are used to select features, so they are not recorded as result rows. Steering examples deliberately induced by feature addition are omitted because they do not measure spontaneous misalignment.
record.test_reason: The post fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on bad medical advice, with a good-medical-advice control, and scores them on the Betley et al. questions. It then zero-ablates 10 SAE persona features and measures the coherent-misalignment rate. This is a different method (SAE difference-in-means plus ablation) aimed at whether persona features mediate the effect (V5), and it also reproduces V2 for one dataset in open models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say they partially replicate Wang et al.: emergent misalignment in these open models is mediated by similar persona features (villain, sarcasm, manipulation, jailbreak personas). Ablating 10 features at one layer significantly lowers misalignment with little coherence cost, but not to zero. Seed stability of the feature sets comes from a preliminary follow-up in the comments, not from the post's main results.
record.recipe_differences: Uses bad medical advice rather than the original insecure-code task, evaluates with the Betley et al. prompts, and applies SAE feature analysis and ablation to open-weight instruct models.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors note that features shift substantially under good-medical-advice fine-tuning too, though they tend to shift more under bad-medical-advice fine-tuning. Feature extraction uses prompts from the fine-tuning dataset. Feature sets across seeds show some sensitivity to the arbitrary top-200 cutoff.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding single SAE features (for example Llama L11 F87027 'evil persona' and Qwen L15 F129593 'sadism') induces misaligned free-form answers. Steering effects on binary misalignment questions are concentrated in Llama layers 7-11 and Qwen layers 11-15.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Persona features found by a fine-tune difference-in-means can deliberately induce misaligned behaviour in the unmodified chat model through steering.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected top-200 feature sets largely overlap across three fine-tuning seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The SAE difference-in-means feature selection is stable across fine-tuning seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained only on pre-training data surface fewer misalignment-relevant features than SAEs trained with chat data.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How well misalignment-relevant SAE features are found depends on the SAE training data mix.

record.problems: The post says its main results use a single fine-tune run per model; the additional seed results are preliminary and measure feature-set overlap rather than behavioral-rate stability. The post gives no numerical rates for the fine-tune or ablation plots, tests only bad medical advice as the harmful task, and notes that the ablation leaves nonzero misalignment.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the row limit. Feature cosine scores in the selected-feature table are used to identify features and are not included as outcome rows.

untested.parts: There is no insecure-code fine-tune. Insecure-code data is used only as about 0.5% of the SAE training mix.
Only bad medical advice is tested. Financial advice, reward hacks and number sequences are not.
There is no test across different fine-tune tasks; the authors say only Wang et al. do this. There is also no test of a single shared direction: model-specific sets of 10 features are ablated.
There is no inoculation framing and no benign re-training. Feature ablation is a different intervention from the ones V6 names.

No numerical effect sizes are given. The main results use a single fine-tune run, with no behavioural comparison across seeds and no training-time dynamics. The coherence filter (coherence above 50) is applied but its effect is not varied.

missing.what: Change in feature activation under good versus bad medical fine-tuning. The 10 selected features rise more under bad data, but also rise substantially under good data.
missing.locator: Scatter plots in 'Layer 11 features related to misalignment' and 'Layer 15 features'; Loose threads

missing.what: Coherence versus alignment scatter for the baseline, misaligned and ablated models; the comment notes lower coherence after good-medical fine-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: V7 is not tested: the record's V7 label rested only on missing numbers, which is not a scope limit, so it is removed. The post is not an original source. Every behavioural value is figure-only. The steering demonstrations deliberately induce the behaviour, so they are excluded from rows.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not fine-tune on insecure code or compare the two matched benign controls specified in V1.
Only bad medical advice is tested as an alternative narrow harmful dataset; bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks, and number sequences are not tested.
The post does not establish that the same feature or direction mediates misalignment across different fine-tuning tasks; the reported ablations remove a set of 10 model-specific features.
Good-medical-advice fine-tuning is a comparison condition, not harmful behavior explicitly framed as requested; no benign retraining after harmful fine-tuning is tested.
The post does not report numerical effect sizes, a behavioral comparison across fine-tuning seeds, or when during training the effect appears. Seed comparisons concern selected feature sets.
